product.title: Indonesian 101 - A2
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from A1 to a solid A2 in Bahasa Indonesia, the direct continuation of the A1 module. Every unit now has two dialogues, one public and one at home or on the phone, each with a word-for-word translation, grammar notes, vocabulary with pronunciation, four keyed exercises and a wave review of earlier units. At this level the affixes stop being something you recognise and become something you build: the me- prefix and its sound rules, spoken nasal forms, object focus, the di- passive, -kan and -i, ber- and saling, ter- and ke-an for accidents, and nouns made with pe-, pe-an, per-an, ke-an and -an. Alongside them come reduplication, yang, because and although, if and if only, reported speech and polite requests, official notices and the formal email, se- words, the many jobs of -nya, numbers for adult life, and the Jakarta Indonesian of gue, lo and the -in verbs. The story follows Sarah back to Indonesia for a new life in a Yogyakarta kampung: registering with the RT, a phone left on the bus, sunrise on the Dieng Plateau, a visa extension, Lebaran with a colleague's family in Klaten, a weekend in Jakarta and Rina's lamaran. Includes an A1 review, an A2 grammar summary and me- verb tables.

blocks.text: At A1 Indonesian got you through the day: a greeting, a price, an *ojek*, a plate of *nasi goreng* and the right way to say "not yet". **A2 is the level at which you stop surviving in Indonesian and start making a life in it.** You rent a house and learn to live next to your landlady. You report to the head of the neighbourhood, open a bank account, extend your visa and find out why the electricity meter is beeping. You are invited home for Lebaran and you know what to say at the door. None of this needs a phrasebook. All of it needs sentences that you build yourself.

Here is the honest news. In A1 the affixes were something you **recognised**: you saw *membeli* and thought "ah, *beli*". **At A2 they become something you build**, and that is where most of the work in this book goes. Units 2 and 3 teach the *me-* prefix and its sound rules, why *pakai* becomes *memakai* and *sapu* becomes *menyapu*, and the spoken forms (*nulis, nyapu, ngambil*) that you will hear far more often than the written ones. Unit 4 turns the sentence round with object focus (*Formulir ini harus Mbak isi*) and the *di-* passive. Units 5 and 6 bring in *-kan* and *-i*, the two suffixes that decide who gets what. Unit 9 shows one root turning into half a dozen nouns, and Unit 11 gives you Indonesian's grammar of bad luck, *ter-* and *ke-…-an*: *tertinggal, kehujanan, kesiangan*.

The rest of A2 is about joining things up and choosing the right voice. Unit 8 doubles words (*sayur-mayur, pelan-pelan, bolak-balik*). Unit 10 is *yang*, the small word behind every description. Units 12 to 14 give you *karena, padahal, kalau, seandainya* and *katanya*, so that your sentences can explain, complain, regret and pass things on. Then two registers pull in opposite directions: **official Indonesian** in Unit 15, the language of notices, forms, bank counters and the formal email (*Yth., Dengan hormat*), and **Jakarta Indonesian** in Unit 19, with *gue, lo*, the *-in* verbs and the particles that no form will ever print. This book teaches both side by side, because you will need both in the same week.

The story picks up fourteen months after A1 ended. In January 2027 Sarah comes back to Indonesia, not to Jakarta this time but to Yogyakarta, where her old company has opened an office and hired her as partnerships coordinator. She rents a small house in a *kampung* near Prawirotaman. Next door lives **Bu Endang**, her landlady, who calls her *Mbak Sarah*, feeds her and has opinions about her empty front yard; with her, most days, is her grandson **Dimas**, ten years old and never short of a question. **Pak Harjo**, the head of the RT, is formal, kind and fond of photocopies. At the office there is **Mas Bayu**, relaxed, Javanese and always joking, and **Mbak Nur**, the office manager, who notices everything. Rina is still in Jakarta, on the other end of the phone, and from Unit 7 on she sounds suspiciously happy.

Over twenty units Sarah furnishes the house (Unit 2), repaints it (Unit 3), reports to Pak Harjo (Unit 4), gets soaked and leaves her phone on a Trans Jogja bus (Unit 11), freezes at dawn on the Dieng Plateau (Unit 13), extends her KITAS (Unit 14) and opens a bank account (Unit 15). She spends Lebaran with Mas Bayu's family in Klaten (Unit 16), learns to cook *gudeg* in Bu Endang's kitchen (Unit 17), and in August takes the train to Jakarta for a long weekend with Rina (Unit 19). The book ends in December, in Unit 20: Sarah tells Pak Hendra about her first year in Yogya, and then sits at the back of the room at Rina's *lamaran* while Andi's family asks formally for her hand.

The method is the one you know from A1: dialogues first, the word-for-word line under every sentence, short explanations and a lot of practice. What is new is the length. There are now **two dialogues in every unit**, the first usually in a public place (a shop, an office, a counter) and the second somewhere looser (the gate, the kitchen, a phone call), because an A2 speaker already has to move between the two.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Give each unit two sittings of about 45 minutes rather than one long evening. The affixes need repetition more than they need explanation.
Read both dialogues **out loud**, twice. Say the *me-* verbs slowly the first time; the sound rules live in your mouth, not on the page.
Make sure the A1 review at the end of this front matter holds no surprises. If three or more of its tables look unfamiliar, go back to A1 first.
Keep the answer key covered until you have finished a whole exercise. Being wrong and finding out why is still the fastest way to learn.

blocks.text: *Selamat belajar*, and welcome to Yogya.

The shape is the one you know from A1, with one big change: every unit now has two dialogues, and more of everything around them. Each unit is built to be finished in two sittings of about 45 minutes, and every part has a job.

items: **Two dialogues.** This is new since A1. The first runs to 13–15 lines and is usually the public scene: a shop, an office, a counter, a meeting. The second, 9–11 lines, moves somewhere else and usually into a looser register: a neighbour at the gate, a phone call, a group chat. Under every line: the natural English, then the word-for-word English.
**Notes.** Six after each dialogue: the things in those lines that would have quietly confused you, and every spoken form with its standard equivalent.
**Grammar boxes.** Three per unit, two after the first dialogue and one after the second, each with a table you can keep.
**Two extra sections.** Word fields, useful phrases and culture that the dialogues only touch on: forms and signs, market words, the Lebaran vocabulary, getting around Jakarta.
**Wave review.** Five lines from two units back, to rebuild from memory.
**Vocabulary.** Every new word, 24–26 per unit, in the order it appears, with the Say it column and the English.

**Exercises and answer key.** Four sets of six items: a translation, a gap fill, a transformation (make it passive, make it formal, say it the Jakarta way) and a word-order puzzle. That is 480 items across the book.

blocks.title: The word-for-word line
items: Hyphens join what is **one word** in Indonesian but several in English: *dibeli* → "is-bought", *kehujanan* → "rained-on", *bukunya* → "book-the" or "book-his", *belikan* → "buy-for".

Particles with no English equivalent stay in square brackets: *[kok] [sih] [dong] [lho] [kan] [deh] [ya] [nih] [-lah] [pun]*. In the Yogyakarta scenes you will also meet the Javanese-flavoured *to* and *nggih*; the notes explain them where they appear, and Unit 19 sorts out the Jakarta ones.

The line is deliberately ungrammatical English. It shows you the order Indonesian thinks in, and at A2 it also shows you where the affixes sit: once you see *dikirimi* as "is-sent-to", the suffix stops being a mystery.

blocks.title: The Say it column
items: Syllables are separated by hyphens and the **stressed syllable is in CAPITALS**, normally the second-last: *pengalaman* puh-nga-LA-man.
**uh** is the schwa, the vowel of "about": *membeli* muhm-BUH-li. When the second-last syllable has a schwa, the stress slides to the last one: *empat* uhm-PAT.
**É** is the *e* of "bed" in a stressed syllable, **é** in an unstressed one: *enak* É-nak, *merah* MÉ-rah, *kesehatan* kuh-sé-HA-tan.
Everything else is spelled as written: *c* is always "ch", *ng* as in "singer", *ny* as in "canyon". Phrases get one block per word: *nasi goreng* NA-si GO-réng.

blocks.text: **The wave.** In A1 the wave was a one-line reminder to re-read an earlier unit. Here it is a table: the third section of every unit gives you five lines from the unit two before it, English on the left, Indonesian on the right. Cover the right-hand column and rebuild each sentence aloud. Units 1 and 2 reach back to the last two units of A1. Five minutes, every unit, and nothing you learned in the rainy season is gone by Lebaran.

blocks.title: Two symbols used throughout
items: ⚠️ — a mistake nearly every foreign learner makes here, or a trap that looks like English. Read these twice.
💬 — the everyday spoken form, next to the written one it replaces. At A2 you need both: the written one for forms and emails, the spoken one to understand your neighbours.

blocks.text: **A realistic pace:** two units a week, one wave review each time and one older unit re-read aloud at the weekend. That is ten weeks to the end of the book. Faster is possible; slower and steadier usually works better.
This is not a lesson. It is the A1 core that every A2 unit uses without explaining it again. Read each table, then do the check under it in your head. If a table holds no surprises, move on.

Numbers and classifiers (A1 Unit 4)

Check: say Rp27.500. (*dua puluh tujuh ribu lima ratus.*) *Se-* means "one" before a unit: *seratus, seribu, sejuta*, never ✗ *satu ratus*. Unit 18 of this book takes the numbers on to fractions, percentages and budgets.
Prepositions (A1 Units 10, 11)

Check: "I'm going to the market first." (*Saya ke pasar dulu.*) *Ke* and *dari* need no verb. ⚠️ *di rumah* (at home) is two words; *dibeli* (is bought) is one. That second *di* is the passive, and it is Unit 4.
Formal and spoken: the swaps that matter most (A1 Unit 20)
Check: say it the way a friend would: *Saya sudah makan, tidak usah.* (*Aku udah makan, nggak usah.*)

A1 also showed you *ber-* (A1 Unit 14), and the *me-*, *di-* and *-kan* you kept seeing on signs (A1 Units 13 and 19), mostly as things to recognise. From Unit 2 of this book you start building them yourself. If three or more tables above feel foreign, spend a week with the A1 units first.

items: **Also in A2:** talking precisely about time with *sejak, selama, … yang lalu, … lagi* and *baru saja* (Unit 1); numbers for adult life, from *setengah* and *sepertiga* to *persen*, the ordinals *kedua, ketiga* and *puluhan, ratusan, sekitar* (Unit 18); and telling a story in order with *pertama-tama, lalu, setelah itu, akhirnya, sejak itu*, plus the formal points of a *lamaran* speech (Unit 20).

head: Root begins with
Prefix

blocks.text: The four sounds that drop are *KaTa SaPu*: *k, t, s, p*. They drop only before a vowel, so loanword clusters stay: *mentransfer, memproduksi, mengkritik*. The prefix *di-* never changes at all: *dibeli, ditulis, disapu, dicat*. 💬 In speech the nasal stays and the *me* goes; roots in *b, d, g, j, l, m, r, w* usually just go bare, and roots in *c* take *ny-* (*nyari, nyuci*).
Five roots, every shape

A dash means the form does not exist or is too rare to learn now. Notice that the Jakarta *-in* does the work of both suffixes: *ngirimin* can be *mengirimkan* (send it) or *mengirimi* (send someone something), and the sentence tells you which. ⚠️ *Ajar* has a second family through *belajar*: *pelajar* is a **student** and *pelajaran* a lesson, while *pengajar* is the teacher.
One verb, seven sentences

head: Shape
Indonesian
English
rows: I'm sending an email to Mbak Nur.
The email was sent by Mas Bayu.
I'll send it to you later.

blocks.text: If you can read all seven and say which ones you would write, you have the centre of A2.

If you have really worked through these twenty units, not just read them, you are at a **solid A2**. You can build *me-* verbs and understand their spoken forms, turn a sentence round with object focus and the passive, ask for favours with *-kan*, explain why something went wrong and whose fault it was not, describe exactly the helmet you lost, fill in a form, read the signs at a bank or a kampung gate, write a short formal email, get through Lebaran as a guest and keep up with friends in Jakarta. That is the Indonesian of someone who lives in the country, not someone visiting it.

What you do not have yet, and what A2 was never meant to give you, is Indonesian for **taking part**: sitting in a meeting and saying what you think at the strength you mean, turning down an invitation without anybody losing face, following the local news, and speaking to an elder or an official with the right respect.

items: **Indonesian 101 · B1** continues directly from this book. In 2028 Sarah coordinates a community-tourism project, a *desa wisata*, in Sumberwangi, a village in the rice fields near Borobudur, working with **Pak Harun** the village head, **Bu Ratna** of the homestay women's group, **Dr. Lestari Wibowo** of UGM and **Yoga**, the intern. On the way: *memper-* verbs, the full passive, abstract nouns, giving opinions and refusing politely, news language, meetings and minutes, respect with *beliau* and *berkenan*, the particles in depth, idioms and proverbs, loanwords, emphasis with *-lah, -kah* and *pun*, the police and the hospital, Rina's wedding, and presenting results on stage.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, four habits that raise your level fastest from here:

items: **Say every new verb three ways.** When you meet a root, say the *me-* form, the *di-* form and the spoken form out loud: *tulis, menulis, ditulis, nulis*. Ten seconds each; after a month the map on the previous page runs by itself.

**Read every sign you pass.** Bank counters, stations, mosques and kampung gates are Unit 15 homework: *Harap antre*, *Tamu wajib lapor 1x24 jam*. Say each one aloud and ask yourself who is being told to do what.
**Listen to people talking to each other**, not to a camera: vlogs of friends, podcasts, long interviews. That is where the *-in* verbs and the particles of Unit 19 live.
**Re-read one unit a week, out loud, in random order.** Twenty weeks later, start again. It costs ten minutes and it keeps everything in this book alive.

blocks.text: And the next time the neighbour leans over the wall and asks *Sudah makan, Mbak?*, answer in a full sentence and ask her something back. That is what A2 was for.
*Sampai jumpa di tingkat B1!*
